result: ASAP2s is a novel voltage indicator containing an R415Q mutation in the S4 helix that exhibits improved voltage responsiveness compared to ASAP1. In HEK293A cells, ASAP2s showed a steady-state fluorescence change of −38.7 ± 1.1% versus −23.3 ± 1.1% for ASAP1 in response to 100 mV depolarization, representing a 66% improvement and the largest amplitude among fluorescent protein-based GEVIs.
evaluation: Claims C16-C22 provide converging evidence from HEK293A cell experiments with specific quantitative measurements, statistical significance (p<0.001), and comparative data to other GEVIs. The mutation is clearly identified, and the improvement is demonstrated with appropriate controls and replication.

result: ASAP2s exhibits faster on-kinetics (5.2 ms) than ArcLight (20 ms) but slower than ASAP1 (2.9 ms), and has a significantly slower off-rate (24 ms) that is ~10-fold slower than ASAP1 while still being rapid enough to track 100 Hz AP trains in single trials.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 present kinetic measurements from HEK293A cells with clear quantitative values referenced in Table 1 and supporting figures. The slower off-rate is demonstrated to be functional for high-frequency tracking, balancing improved detection with adequate temporal resolution.

result: ASAP2s matches ASAP1 in brightness under both one- and two-photon illumination when expressed in HEK293-Kir2.1 cells, with both indicators maximally excited at approximately 920 nm under two-photon illumination.
evaluation: Claims C28-C30 are supported by brightness measurements in HEK293-Kir2.1 cells and two-photon excitation spectra (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B). The comparison to EGFP as a standard and consistency with published reports strengthens the findings.

result: Under one-photon widefield microscopy, ASAP1 and ASAP2s photobleach similarly to each other and to ArcLight, but more slowly than ASAP1::EGFP. Both ASAP indicators show partial fluorescence recovery (8.9-22.4%) after dark incubation, with greater recovery after longer incubation periods. Similar recovery patterns are observed under two-photon illumination (20-25% after 5 min).
evaluation: Claims C31-C36 present systematic photobleaching characterization under both one- and two-photon conditions with quantitative measurements and appropriate controls. The reversible photobleaching phenomenon is documented with specific recovery percentages and time dependencies.

result: In human embryonic stem cell-derived cardiomyocytes, ASAP2s exhibited superior response amplitude (−45.1 ± 1.5%) compared to ASAP1 (−24.0 ± 1.8%) and ArcLight (−32.9 ± 1.8%) when reporting cardiac action potentials. The faster kinetics of ASAP indicators compared to ArcLight enabled shorter time to peak.
evaluation: Claims C37-C40 demonstrate ASAP2s performance in a physiologically relevant cell type with specific measurements, error estimates, and comparative data. The findings are consistent with HEK293A cell results and supported by figures and video data.

result: ASAP2s localizes efficiently to the plasma membrane in cultured neurons and reports action potentials with −12.2 ± 0.5% fluorescence change compared to −8.6 ± 0.3% for ASAP1, representing a 42% improvement in response amplitude. The combination of higher amplitude and longer duration resulted in 90% greater integrated fluorescence change.
evaluation: Claims C41-C46 provide evidence from neuronal cultures with confocal imaging confirming membrane localization and quantitative measurements of AP responses. The integrated fluorescence metric appropriately captures the combined effect of amplitude and duration improvements.

result: In Drosophila L2 neurons, ASAP2s produced significantly larger responses than ASAP1 (37% increase for depolarizations, 39% for hyperpolarizations) when imaging voltage dynamics in response to visual stimuli, though with slightly slower kinetics. ArcLight showed similar amplitudes to ASAP1 but significantly slower kinetics. All three indicators enabled high SNR imaging for over 30 minutes.
evaluation: Claims C47-C54 demonstrate ASAP2s performance in an intact organism with appropriate anatomical context, quantitative comparisons, and long-term stability data. The in vivo validation strengthens the overall characterization of the indicator.

result: Opsin-based voltage indicators (Ace2N-2AA-mNeon and MacQ-mCitrine) showed minimal or undetectable responses to visual stimulation in Drosophila L2 neurons under two-photon illumination. Unexpectedly, Ace2N-2AA-mNeon exhibited inverted response polarity compared to one-photon illumination.
evaluation: Claims C55-C57 document the poor performance of opsin-based indicators under two-photon conditions with specific observations across multiple excitation wavelengths. The inverted polarity finding is unexpected but robustly demonstrated, highlighting limitations of these indicator classes.

result: GCaMP6f showed substantially larger peak response amplitude and higher SNR than voltage sensors in Drosophila L2 neurons, but the response was not transient and continued throughout the stimulus duration. Calcium indicator traces do not correlate with GEVI traces in a simple manner.
evaluation: Claims C58-C60 provide important comparative data showing fundamental differences between calcium and voltage imaging. The observation that calcium traces don't simply correlate with voltage traces illustrates the distinct information provided by each approach.

result: In organotypic hippocampal slice cultures using RAMP microscopy, ASAP2s produced a fluorescence change of −15.0 ± 0.6% in response to action potentials, representing a 79% improvement over ASAP1 (−8.4 ± 0.5%). These two-photon response amplitudes are remarkably similar to one-photon responses.
evaluation: Claims C61-C65 demonstrate successful two-photon voltage imaging in brain tissue with quantitative measurements and statistical significance. The preservation of response amplitude between one- and two-photon excitation is an important validation of the indicator's properties.

result: ASAP2s can report spontaneous action potentials and both ASAP2s and ASAP1 can reliably detect subthreshold depolarization and hyperpolarization waveforms in single trials in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures.
evaluation: Claims C66-C67 extend the characterization to spontaneous activity and subthreshold events, demonstrating the breadth of voltage dynamics that can be monitored. The single-trial detection capability is crucial for practical applications.

result: At 925 Hz imaging frequency in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures, ASAP2s achieved a d' value of 53.9 ± 3.2 compared to 15.0 ± 3.7 for ASAP1 (p<0.0001). Both values indicate >99% detection rate and false-positive rate per frame <10⁻⁸.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 provide rigorous quantification of spike detectability using an established framework (Wilt et al., 2013). The large difference in d' values between ASAP2s and ASAP1 with statistical significance demonstrates substantial improvement in detection capability.

result: In organotypic hippocampal slice cultures at 3700 Hz sampling, ASAP1 exhibited AP-induced transients with time-to-peak of 3.1 ms and duration of 3.8 ms, while ASAP2s showed slower kinetics with time-to-peak of 6.0 ms and duration of 21.1 ms.
evaluation: Claims C71-C73 provide detailed kinetic characterization in brain tissue that is consistent with measurements in HEK293A cells. The high-speed imaging (3700 Hz) enables accurate temporal resolution of the indicators' response properties.

result: ASAP2s signal amplitudes remained relatively constant across scanning frequencies from 231-3700 Hz in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures, while ASAP2s showed higher SNR than ASAP1 at all frequencies. ASAP2s SNR increased with decreasing frequency (10.0 ± 1.6 at 231 Hz vs 5.4 ± 0.4 at 3700 Hz), while ASAP1 SNR remained constant at ~5.
evaluation: Claims C74-C78 systematically characterize the relationship between scanning frequency and performance metrics. The findings provide practical guidance for optimizing imaging parameters and demonstrate ASAP2s' advantage for sub-kilohertz imaging.

result: During high-frequency spike trains in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures, fluorescence did not recover to baseline between peaks, reducing response amplitude of subsequent spikes. Detectability (d') decreased with increasing AP frequency. ASAP2s reported spike trains with larger d' than ASAP1 for frequencies up to 30 Hz, but at 100 Hz both indicators showed similar and strongly reduced d' values.
evaluation: Claims C79-C82 characterize performance limitations during high-frequency activity, which is important for understanding the indicators' operational range. The frequency-dependent reduction in detectability is expected given the kinetics and is appropriately documented.

result: ASAP2f performed similarly to ASAP1 across all metrics in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures, including brightness, peak amplitude, SNR, kinetics, and response to spike trains.
evaluation: Claim C83 provides comparative data for ASAP2f, establishing that it performs similarly to ASAP1 and thus ASAP2s represents a clear improvement over both. The comprehensive comparison across multiple metrics strengthens this conclusion.

result: Ace2N-4AA-mNeon produced a fluorescence change of only −1.8 ± 0.4% in response to 100 mV step depolarization in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures under two-photon illumination.
evaluation: Claim C84 documents the poor performance of an opsin-based indicator under two-photon conditions in brain tissue, consistent with findings in Drosophila. The small response amplitude makes this indicator unsuitable for the application.

result: ASAP2s enables single-voxel, single-trial spike detection in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures with SNR of 2.2 ± 0.2 at 925 Hz, compared to 1.1 ± 0.1 for ASAP1. Binning four timepoints (effective 200 μs dwell time) more than doubled SNR. With ASAP2s, d' for single-voxel spike detection was 17.5 ± 1.2, indicating >99% detection rate and <10⁻⁸ false-positive rate.
evaluation: Claims C85-C89 demonstrate a critical milestone: reliable single-voxel, single-trial spike detection. The quantitative metrics (SNR, d') with appropriate statistical analysis support the conclusion that FEVIR using ASAP2s can reliably report APs even at single-voxel resolution.

result: ASAP2s-powered FEVIR enables subcellular voltage imaging in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures, revealing that AP-evoked optical signals gradually decreased with distance from soma (37.6 ± 7.3% lower at 144.3 ± 3.5 μm), with mean conduction velocity of 0.16 ± 0.03 m/s. APs in dendrites were broader than in soma, consistent with previous electrophysiological reports.
evaluation: Claims C90-C95 demonstrate subcellular voltage imaging capabilities with measurements of AP propagation that are consistent with published electrophysiological data. This validation against established findings strengthens confidence in the optical measurements and demonstrates the utility of the approach.

result: Previous studies demonstrated that many GEVIs show >75% reduction in response amplitude under two-photon versus one-photon excitation, while ASAP1 was unique in maintaining similar response amplitudes under both illumination modes.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 establish important context from prior work (Brinks et al., 2015) that motivates the choice of ASAP1 as the template for improvement. This background is appropriately cited and supports the rationale for the study.

result: The resting membrane potential, membrane capacitance, and input resistance of GEVI-expressing and untransfected neurons were statistically indistinguishable in organotypic hippocampal slice cultures.
evaluation: Claim C98 provides important control data showing that GEVI expression does not perturb basic electrophysiological properties of neurons. This is supported by measurements in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and is consistent with previous ASAP1 characterization.

result: Opsin-based GEVIs (single-domain opsins and FRET-opsin/electrochromic FRET indicators) show greatly attenuated responses under two-photon microscopy compared to one-photon microscopy, making them less suitable for two-photon applications despite some showing larger one-photon responses than ASAP2s.
evaluation: Claims C99-C101 synthesize findings from the current study and cited literature to conclude that opsin-based indicators are poorly suited for two-photon imaging. The evidence from multiple indicator classes and experimental systems supports this general conclusion.

result: The combination of ASAP2s and fast two-photon imaging methods (FEVIR) enables robust single-trial detection of action potentials in organotypic slice cultures, two-photon imaging of graded potentials in organotypic slice cultures and Drosophila, and detection of neural electrical activity with subcellular spatial resolution and millisecond-timescale precision.
evaluation: Claims C2-C4 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript. The combination of improved indicator properties and advanced imaging methodology achieves capabilities not previously demonstrated.

result: Genetically encoded calcium indicators like GCaMP6f are commonly used to detect neuronal activity but have limitations: calcium concentration is not directly related to membrane potential, they cannot effectively report hyperpolarizations and subthreshold depolarizations, and their slow kinetics limit temporal precision and ability to track fast spike trains.
evaluation: Claims C5-C9 establish the motivation for voltage imaging by describing well-established limitations of calcium indicators. These statements are supported by appropriate citations to the literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

result: While GEVIs have been developed and used for one-photon imaging in vivo, two-photon microscopy is preferred for in vivo studies due to deeper penetration and lower background/phototoxicity. However, prior to this study, GEVI-based two-photon voltage imaging in intact tissue had only been demonstrated with either low temporal resolution (<100 Hz), low spatial resolution, or both, and robust single-trial imaging with millisecond and cellular/subcellular resolution had not been reported.
evaluation: Claims C10-C14 establish the gap in the field that this study addresses. The statements are supported by appropriate citations and accurately describe the state of the field prior to this work, establishing the novelty and significance of the current findings.

result: The probability of correctly identifying spikes from optical noise is higher for sensors with larger response amplitudes, greater brightness, and longer signal decay (slower off-rate).
evaluation: Claim C15 states an established principle from Wilt et al., 2013 that guides the design criteria for ASAP2s. This theoretical framework is appropriately cited and provides the rationale for targeting specific indicator properties.
